In [[mathematics]], specifically in [[algebraic geometry]], '''rigid cohomology''' is a [[P-adic cohomology|{{math|''p''}}-adic cohomology]] theory introduced by [[Pierre Berthelot]] in 1986.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Berthelot |first=Pierre |date=1986 |title=Géométrie rigide et cohomologie des variétés algébriques de caractéristique {{math|''p''}} |url=https://www.numdam.org/item/?id=MSMF_1986_2_23__R3_0 |journal=Mémoires de la Société Mathématique de France |series=Nouvelle série |issue=23 |pages=7–32 |issn=0037-9484 |mr=865810}}</ref> It extends [[crystalline cohomology]] to [[scheme (mathematics)|schemes]] that need not be proper or [[smooth scheme|smooth]], and extends [[Monsky–Washnitzer cohomology]] to non-[[affine variety|affine varieties]].

For a scheme <math>X</math> of finite type over a [[perfect field]] <math>k</math>, there are rigid cohomology groups <math>H^i_{\textrm{rig}}(X/K)</math> which are finite dimensional vector spaces over the field <math>K</math> of fractions of the ring of Witt vectors of <math>k</math>. More generally, one can define rigid cohomology with compact supports, or with support on a closed subscheme, or with coefficients in an overconvergent [[crystal (mathematics)|isocrystal]]. 
If <math>X</math> is smooth and proper over <math>k</math>, the rigid cohomology groups are the same as the crystalline cohomology groups.

The name "rigid cohomology" comes from its relation to [[rigid analytic space]]s. 

In 2006, [[Kiran Kedlaya]] used rigid cohomology to give a new proof of the [[Weil conjectures]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kedlaya |first=Kiran S. |date=2006 |title=Fourier transforms and p-adic 'Weil II' |journal=Compositio Mathematica |volume=142 |issue=6 |pages=1426–1450| doi=10.1112/S0010437X06002338 |doi-broken-date=10 August 2026 |mr=2278753 |issn=0010-437X |arxiv=math/0210149 |s2cid=5233570}}</ref>
